title: NCLT Pulls Up SpiceJet Over Last-Minute Settlement Tactics in Insolvency Cases
excerpt: India's aviation tribunal reprimands the budget carrier for wasting court time as it settles just one of eight lessor claims, raising questions about whether the airline is using insolvency proceedings as a negotiating tool.
body:
• The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has reprimanded SpiceJet for repeatedly offering last-minute settlements in insolvency proceedings, calling the practice a waste of judicial resources.
  • The airline has settled with only one of eight aircraft lessors who have filed insolvency petitions, despite raising ₹3,000 crore through a qualified institutional placement in 2024.
  • Legal experts say SpiceJet's pattern highlights a growing trend of companies using the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) forum to pressure creditors into accepting reduced terms.
  • Multiple insolvency claims from Irish lessors and other creditors remain pending, with the airline's fleet expansion plans hanging in the balance.

The National Company Law Tribunal has pulled up SpiceJet for wasting the court's time by offering last-minute settlement proposals in insolvency proceedings brought by aircraft lessors, adding to the budget carrier's mounting legal and financial troubles.

A Pattern of Last-Minute Offers

SpiceJet has faced a wave of insolvency petitions from aircraft lessors over the past two years. The airline's strategy has followed a consistent pattern: as hearings approach, SpiceJet's counsel requests adjournments, citing ongoing settlement talks. When pressured by the tribunal, the airline produces settlement offers — often at the last minute — that creditors have repeatedly rejected as inadequate.

The NCLT bench noted that the airline's approach amounts to using the insolvency forum as leverage rather than engaging in genuine settlement negotiations. The tribunal has encouraged SpiceJet to resolve disputes with lessors, but patience appears to be wearing thin.

"SpiceJet's case highlights a growing trend where creditors use the IBC forum to pressure corporate debtors into settlement. The IBC is meant to resolve genuine insolvency cases, not to serve as a tool for creditors to force settlements."

— Alay Razvi, Managing Partner, Accord Juris

One Settlement, Seven Pending

Despite raising ₹3,000 crore (approximately $360 million) through a qualified institutional placement (QIP), SpiceJet has settled only a fraction of its outstanding lessor disputes. The airline reached agreements with Celestial Aviation, Alterna Aircraft, Raymach Technologies, and Aircastle — the last withdrawing its insolvency case after a $5.6 million settlement. It also settled a $131.85 million dispute with Babcock & Brown Aircraft Management.

But multiple claims remain active. Three Ireland-based lessors — NGF Alpha, NGF Genesis, and NGF Charlie — have filed petitions claiming combined dues of $12.68 million, alleging that SpiceJet defaulted on rental payments and even stripped parts from five leased Boeing 737 freighters. Indonesia's PT BBN Airlines has also filed over $5.94 million in unpaid lease rentals.

Shannon Engine Support Limited and Techjockey Infotech have pending pleas as well. Wilmington Trust and Willis Lease Finance are appealing NCLT dismissals at the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

The Broader IBC Question

SpiceJet's case has reignited debate about whether the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, designed to resolve genuine insolvency situations, is being misused as a debt-recovery mechanism. Legal experts note the airline business is structurally unusual — liabilities routinely exceed assets — making it a poor fit for standard insolvency frameworks.

"SpiceJet's case is unusual, as multiple IBC proceedings have been filed against the airline by both operational and financial creditors in a short period."

— Kalpit Khandelwal, Partner, Aekom Legal

None of the insolvency claims against SpiceJet has advanced to full corporate insolvency resolution proceedings (CIRP), where an independent resolution professional would take control of the company. The tribunal has consistently given the airline time to negotiate, but the repeated adjournments and partial settlements suggest a company playing for time rather than demonstrating financial recovery.

Fleet Ambitions vs. Financial Reality

SpiceJet Chairman Ajay Singh has stated the airline aims to expand its fleet to 100 aircraft by 2026. The airline had planned to return 36 grounded aircraft to service, but court orders mandating the grounding of leased engines due to unpaid dues have complicated those plans.

The QIP funds were explicitly earmarked for settling liabilities with creditors, clearing statutory dues of ₹601.5 crore, and funding operational recovery. Yet the pace of settlements has lagged behind the scale of outstanding claims, raising questions about whether the capital raise is sufficient to stabilize the airline's operations.

What's Next

The NCLT has scheduled further hearings on the pending lessor claims. If SpiceJet fails to reach settlements, the tribunal could admit one or more petitions into CIRP — a scenario that would effectively place the airline under external management and could trigger a cascade of creditor actions. For now, SpiceJet continues to walk a tightrope between settlement negotiations and the threat of formal insolvency proceedings.
